intro: The first chapters of Genesis tell very old stories. A garden is lost. Heavenly beings cross into the human world. A great flood comes, and one family is kept safe. Michael Heiser, a scholar who read the Bible's old languages, saw a pattern in these chapters. He called them rebellions, times when someone went against God's plan.

In this unit you read two of those stories closely: the serpent in Eden (Genesis 3) and the sons of God before the Flood (Genesis 6). You learn the old Hebrew words, what Heiser thought they meant, and how other readers see them. You do not have to pick a side. You learn to explain each reading fairly.

By the end, you will be able to retell both stories in order. You will name the verses each reading uses. You will explain words like nachash, Nephilim and covenant. And you will show how careful readers build a case from clues.
bigQuestion: How did Heiser read the first rebellions in Genesis, and how do other readers read the same verses?

timeline.t: Genesis 2: God plants a garden in Eden and puts the first man there
Genesis 3: the serpent speaks, the people choose, and they leave the garden
Genesis 6:1–4: the sons of God take wives, and the Nephilim are on the earth
Genesis 6–9: the Flood comes, Noah's family is kept safe, and the rainbow is given
Genesis 11: people build the tower of Babel, the third rebellion
The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36) retells Genesis 6 (c. 300–200 BCE)
The Book of Jubilees also says the angels took wives
Revelation calls the old serpent the Devil and Satan (Revelation 12:9)
Augustine teaches the line of Seth reading in City of God
Heiser publishes Reversing Hermon, on Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch

words.d: refusing to follow the one in charge; Heiser used it for three stories in Genesis
the place in Genesis where God planted a garden
Heiser's name for God's heavenly family or court of spirit beings
the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3; related words mean giving omens and bronze
heavenly beings in the Bible who guard holy places
children and the families that come after them
the beings in Genesis 6:2 who took wives; readers disagree about who they were
a group named in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33; many translations call them giants
1 Enoch's name for the heavenly beings who came down to earth
the Greek word in 2 Peter 2:4 for the dark place where angels who sinned are kept
a large box-shaped boat; in Genesis, the boat Noah built
a serious promise that binds two sides together

test.q: Which three chapters of Genesis hold Heiser's three rebellions?
test.why: Heiser pointed to Genesis 3 (Eden), 6 (sons of God) and 11 (Babel).

choices: The garden of God and the holy mountain of God
test.why: Ezekiel 28:13–14 calls Eden the garden of God and speaks of the holy mountain of God.

test.q: Why did Heiser connect nachash with shining?
choices: Because Genesis says the serpent glowed
Because a related Hebrew word means bronze
test.why: A word related to nachash means bronze, a shiny metal.

test.q: Which book first names the old serpent as Satan, among the books in this unit?
test.why: Revelation 12:9 calls the old serpent the Devil and Satan; Genesis 3 gives no name.

test.q: Who guarded the way to the tree of life?
test.why: Genesis 3:24 says cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way.

test.q: What does Genesis 3:15 say will happen to the serpent's head?
choices: The woman's offspring will bruise it
It will be hidden in the ark
test.why: Genesis 3:15 says the woman's offspring will bruise the serpent's head.

test.q: Which book uses sons of God for beings in God's heavenly court?
test.why: Job 1:6 and 38:7 use sons of God for heavenly beings.

test.q: What is the oldest known reading of Genesis 6, found in 1 Enoch and Jubilees?
choices: The sons of God were kings
The sons of God were heavenly beings
The sons of God were Noah's sons
The sons of God were Seth's family
test.why: 1 Enoch and Jubilees, from before the time of Jesus, read them as heavenly beings.

test.q: What does 1 Enoch call the heavenly beings who came down?
Which leader taught the line of Seth reading in City of God?
test.why: Augustine taught this reading around 420 CE.

test.q: Which reading says the sons of God were proud human rulers?
test.why: The kings reading sees them as powerful rulers, like the Targum Onqelos's sons of great men.

test.q: Which two New Testament passages did Heiser use about angels who sinned?
test.why: Heiser pointed to 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6.

test.q: Which verse do many readers who disagree with Heiser point to?
test.why: Many who reject the heavenly beings reading point to Matthew 22:30.

test.q: About how long was Noah's ark in feet?
test.why: 300 cubits at about 18 inches each is about 450 feet.

test.q: What was the sign of God's covenant with Noah?
test.why: Genesis 9:13 names the bow in the cloud as the sign of the covenant.

write.prompt: Pick one question: Who was the serpent in Eden? or Who were the sons of God in Genesis 6? Cite two or three passages from the unit (for example Genesis 3:1, Ezekiel 28:13, Job 38:7, 1 Enoch 6). Explain what each text says, how Heiser read it, and how one other reading sees it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every text you use.
Say who holds each view: Heiser, Augustine, 1 Enoch, many Christians or many Jewish readers.
Explain each reading fairly, as its own readers would.
Use the unit's words, like nachash, sons of God and Nephilim, and say what they mean.

title: Three Rebellions

chapters.title: Eden and the Shining One
chapters.bigQuestion: Who was the serpent in the garden of Eden, and why do readers answer that question in different ways?

story.title: The Snake on the Kitchen Table
story.kicker: Two cousins disagree about a snake in a very old story, so they open the book and read it together.
paragraphs: Maya and her cousin Leo sat at the kitchen table after dinner. Leo had a picture book of Bible stories. On one page, a green snake hung from a tree in a garden. "It is just a snake," Leo said. "A snake that could talk." Maya shook her head. "My teacher said it might be something else."

Leo's grandmother heard them. She did not pick a side. Instead she brought a real Bible to the table. "Let's see what the words say," she said. "Then you can see why people read them in different ways." She turned to the book of Genesis, chapter 3.

They read the first verse slowly. The serpent was clever, more than any wild animal. It spoke to the woman. It asked her a tricky question about what God had said. Leo pointed at the page. "See? It says animal." Maya pointed too. "It says it was more clever than the animals. And snakes do not talk."

Grandma smiled. "You both noticed something true," she said. "Some readers think this was a snake in a teaching story. A scholar named Michael Heiser thought it was a shining spirit being. He studied the old Hebrew words to find out." Leo leaned in. "What Hebrew words?" Grandma opened her notebook. "Let's find out together."
story.think: Maya and Leo each noticed something real in the words. What is a good way to talk with someone who reads a story differently than you do?

lessons.title: Three Stories Go Wrong
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser saw three early stories in Genesis where things go wrong: Eden, the sons of God, and the tower of Babel.
reading: Genesis is the first book of the Bible. Its early chapters tell how the world began. Michael Heiser was a scholar who read the Bible in its old languages. In his book The Unseen Realm (2015), he pointed to three stories in these chapters. In each one, someone goes against God's plan.

The first story is in Genesis 3, in the garden of Eden. The second is in Genesis 6, where the sons of God come down to people. The third is in Genesis 11, at the tower of Babel. Heiser called each one a *rebellion*. A rebellion is when someone refuses to follow the one in charge.

Heiser thought these three stories work together. He said they help explain why the world in the Bible is so troubled. Not every reader groups the stories this way. Many readers see them as separate stories. This course looks closely at how Heiser put them together.

words.d: refusing to follow the one in charge; Heiser used it for three stories in Genesis
the first book of the Bible, which tells stories of beginnings

look.title: Where the Three Stories Are
look.cite: Genesis 3, 6 and 11; Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (2015)
look.prompt: Which story comes first in Genesis? How many chapters are there between the first and the last story?

check.q: In which book are all three of Heiser's rebellion stories found?
check.why: All three stories come from Genesis, chapters 3, 6 and 11.

check.q: Which story did Heiser count as the third rebellion?
check.why: Heiser counted the tower of Babel in Genesis 11 as the third rebellion.

check.q: What does the word rebellion mean in this lesson?
choices: Refusing to follow the one in charge
check.why: A rebellion is when someone refuses to follow the one in charge.

lessons.title: Who Was Michael Heiser?
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser was a scholar who read the Bible's old languages and wrote about its unseen world.
reading: Michael Heiser lived from 1963 to 2023. He was a *scholar*. A scholar is a person who studies one subject very closely for many years. Heiser studied the Hebrew Bible and other old writings from the same part of the world.

Heiser could read *Hebrew*, the language most of the Old Testament was first written in. He believed reading the old words helps a reader see details that a translation can hide. He wrote books such as The Unseen Realm (2015) and Supernatural (2015). He also hosted the Naked Bible Podcast.

In this course, you study how Heiser read the Bible. You are not asked to agree or disagree. You learn what the text says, what Heiser thought, and how other readers see it. That is what careful students of any old book do.

words.d: a person who studies one subject very closely for many years
the language most of the Old Testament was first written in

look.title: Two Ways to Read
look.text: Picture two students with the same story. One reads it in English only. The other also looks up each old Hebrew word in a word book. The second student finds that one word can mean more than one thing.
look.prompt: What could the second student notice that the first student might miss?

check.q: What is a scholar?
choices: A person who writes only poems
A person who studies one subject closely for many years
check.why: A scholar studies one subject very closely for a long time, as Heiser did with the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: Which language was most of the Old Testament first written in?
check.why: Most of the Old Testament was first written in Hebrew, which Heiser could read.

check.q: What is your job as a student in this course?
choices: To memorize the whole book of Genesis
To decide that Heiser was wrong
To decide that Heiser was right
To learn what the text says and how different readers see it
check.why: The course studies what the text says, what Heiser thought and how others read it.

lessons.title: A Garden in Eden
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 2 says God planted a garden in Eden, with trees, a river and people to care for it.
reading: Genesis 2 tells of a *garden* God planted in a place called *Eden*. The story says it grew every tree that was good to look at and good for food. In the middle stood the tree of life. There was also the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden. Then it split into four rivers. Genesis names two that readers still know today, the Tigris and the Euphrates. These rivers flow through the land that is now Iraq.

The story says God put the first man in the garden to work it and keep it. God told him he could eat from every tree but one. That one was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This rule becomes very important in Genesis 3.

words.d: the place in Genesis where God planted a garden
a planted place with trees and plants; in Genesis, the home God made in Eden

look.title: The Garden Is Planted
look.text: God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and put the man there. God made every tree grow that was lovely to see and good to eat. The tree of life was in the middle of the garden, and so was the tree of knowing good and evil.
look.cite: Genesis 2:8–9, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Name the two special trees in the middle of the garden.

check.q: Which two rivers named in Genesis 2 do people still know today?
check.why: Genesis 2 names the Tigris and the Euphrates, which flow through what is now Iraq.

check.q: Which tree was the man told not to eat from?
choices: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil
check.why: Genesis 2 says God told the man not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

check.q: What job did God give the man in the garden, in Genesis 2?
choices: To work it and keep it
check.why: The story says God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it.

lessons.title: The Garden and the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: Ezekiel 28 calls Eden both the garden of God and the holy mountain of God.
reading: Genesis is not the only book that mentions Eden. The prophet *Ezekiel* wrote about it too. In Ezekiel 28, he speaks a poem to the king of Tyre, a rich city by the sea. The poem uses pictures from Eden to describe the king.

Ezekiel 28:13 says, "Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God." Verse 14 speaks of "the holy mountain of God." In this poem, Eden is a garden and also a mountain. Heiser noticed this. He thought it showed that Eden was more than a farm. It was the place where God lived.

Other readers point out that the poem is about a human king. They read the Eden words as a picture of the king's pride. Heiser agreed the poem speaks to the king. But he thought it also looks back to a proud being in Eden. Readers still discuss this.

words.d: a prophet of Israel whose book is in the Bible; chapter 28 mentions Eden
a high, holy place in the Bible where God is pictured as living

look.title: Eden in Ezekiel
look.text: Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering.
look.prompt: What two words does Ezekiel put right after the name Eden?

check.q: Who is Ezekiel 28 spoken to?
check.why: Ezekiel 28 is a poem spoken to the king of Tyre that uses pictures from Eden.

check.q: What two things does Ezekiel 28 call Eden?
choices: The garden of God and the holy mountain of God
check.why: Ezekiel 28:13 says the garden of God, and 28:14 speaks of the holy mountain of God.

check.q: How do some other readers understand the Eden words in Ezekiel 28?
choices: As a story about the Flood
As a picture of a human king's pride
As a list of Eden's rivers
check.why: Other readers see the Eden words as a picture that describes the king of Tyre's pride.

lessons.title: A Place to Meet God
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read Eden as God's home, where God, people and heavenly beings could meet.
reading: Genesis 3:8 says the man and woman heard God walking in the garden in the cool of the day. In this story, God is close by. People and God share the same place. Many readers find this a warm and peaceful picture.

Heiser read Eden as God's home on earth. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he wrote that God's home also had heavenly beings. He called this group the *divine council*. It is like God's family or court in the unseen world. He thought Eden was where heaven and earth met.

Not all readers see a council in Eden. Many read Genesis 2 and 3 as a story only about God and the first people. Heiser's idea came from reading Genesis next to Ezekiel 28 and Psalm 82. You will read more about the divine council in other units.

words.d: Heiser's name for God's heavenly family or court of spirit beings
spirit beings the Bible pictures in God's presence, such as angels

look.title: Two Pictures of Eden
look.text: Picture A: a quiet garden where only God and two people meet. Picture B: a garden on a holy mountain, where God meets people and heavenly beings serve around God. Heiser drew Picture B. Many other readers draw Picture A.
look.prompt: Which verses from this lesson helped Heiser draw Picture B?

check.q: What does Genesis 3:8 say the man and woman heard?
check.why: Genesis 3:8 says they heard God walking in the garden in the cool of the day.

check.q: What did Heiser call the group of heavenly beings around God?
check.why: Heiser called God's heavenly family or court the divine council.

check.q: How do many other readers see Genesis 2 and 3?
choices: As a story only about God and the first people
check.why: Many readers see no council in Eden and read it as a story about God and the first people.

lessons.title: The Word Nachash
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew word for serpent, nachash, sounds like words for giving omens and for shining bronze.
reading: In Genesis 3, the Hebrew word for the serpent is *nachash*. Most English Bibles translate it as serpent or snake. That is its usual meaning. Heiser, who read Hebrew, looked at other words that sound the same or come from the same letters.

One related word means to give *omens*. An omen is a sign people once used to try to tell the future. Another related word means bronze, a shiny metal. Heiser wrote that these links could point to a being that shines and gives secret messages.

Word links like these are clues, not proof. Hebrew has many words that look alike. Heiser knew this. He said the context, the story around the word, matters most. He used these clues together with other passages, like Ezekiel 28.

words.d: the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3; related words mean giving omens and bronze
signs people once used to try to tell the future

look.title: One Word, Three Clues
look.text: Clue 1: nachash as a noun means serpent. Clue 2: a related word means to give omens. Clue 3: a related word means bronze, a shiny metal. Heiser thought the serpent in Eden might carry all three ideas at once.
look.prompt: Put the three clues together. What kind of being do they describe?

check.q: What does nachash usually mean?
check.why: Nachash is the usual Hebrew word for serpent or snake.

check.q: Which shiny metal is linked to a word related to nachash?
check.why: A related Hebrew word means bronze, a shiny metal, which Heiser linked to shining.

check.q: What did Heiser say matters most when reading a word?
choices: The context, the story around the word
The longest meaning in a dictionary
check.why: Heiser said word links are clues and the context around the word matters most.

lessons.title: A Shining One or a Snake?
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the serpent as a shining spirit being; other readers see an ordinary snake in a teaching story.
reading: Heiser thought the serpent was not an ordinary snake. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he argued it was a spirit being from God's council. He pointed to clues. It talks. It knows what God said. Ezekiel 28 describes a shining being in Eden. He called it a *shining one*.

Other readers see it differently. Genesis 3:1 compares the serpent to the wild animals God made. Many Jewish and Christian readers take this as a real snake. Some scholars read Genesis 3 as a *teaching story*. In that reading, a talking snake teaches a lesson about choices.

Both readings start from the same verses. They notice different details. Heiser focused on the talking and on Ezekiel 28. Others focus on the word animal. Careful students can explain both readings fairly.

words.d: Heiser's description of the serpent as a bright spirit being, not an ordinary snake
a story told mainly to teach a lesson about how to live

look.title: The Clever Serpent
look.text: The serpent was more clever than any wild animal the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, "Did God really say you may not eat from any tree in the garden?"
look.cite: Genesis 3:1, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Find one detail a reader might use to say it was a snake, and one detail Heiser might use to say it was more.

check.q: What did Heiser argue the serpent was?
choices: A spirit being from God's council
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser argued the serpent was a spirit being, a shining one.

check.q: Which detail in Genesis 3:1 do many readers use to say it was a real snake?
choices: It is compared to the wild animals
check.why: Genesis 3:1 compares the serpent to the wild animals, which many readers take to mean a real snake.

check.q: What is a teaching story?
choices: A song sung at a temple
A story told mainly to teach a lesson
check.why: A teaching story is told mainly to teach a lesson, which is how some scholars read Genesis 3.

lessons.title: Later Readers Name the Serpent
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 3 never names the serpent, but Revelation 12:9 and later Christians call it Satan.
reading: Read Genesis 3 closely, and you will notice something. The serpent is never given a name. It is only called the serpent. The name *Satan* does not appear in the Eden story at all.

Many centuries later came *Revelation*, the last book of the Christian Bible. It speaks of a great dragon. Revelation 12:9 calls it "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan." Because of this verse, many Christians came to see the Eden serpent as Satan.

Heiser agreed that the New Testament links the two. But he wanted readers to see Genesis on its own terms first. Some Jewish readers do not link the serpent to Satan. Others read it simply as a snake. Knowing which book says what helps you keep the readings clear.

words.d: a name used in later books of the Bible for a leading enemy of God; it is not used in Genesis 3
the last book of the Christian New Testament

look.title: The Old Serpent
look.text: And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.
look.prompt: Which three names does this verse give the dragon?

check.q: Does Genesis 3 give the serpent a name?
choices: Yes, it calls it the king of Tyre
No, it is only called the serpent
Yes, it calls it the Devil
check.why: Genesis 3 only calls it the serpent; the name Satan does not appear there.

check.q: Which verse calls the old serpent the Devil and Satan?
check.why: Revelation 12:9 calls the dragon that old serpent, the Devil and Satan.

check.q: What is Revelation?
choices: The first book of the Bible
The last book of the Christian New Testament
check.why: Revelation is the last book of the Christian New Testament.

lessons.title: The Choice
lessons.mainIdea: In Genesis 3, the woman and the man choose to eat from the one tree God said not to eat from.
reading: The serpent told the woman she would not die if she ate the fruit. It said she would be like God, knowing good and evil. The woman saw that the fruit looked good. She ate some. She gave some to the man, and he ate too.

Then the story says their eyes were opened. They saw they were naked and made coverings from fig leaves. When they heard God in the garden, they hid. God called out, "Where art thou?" The man and the woman each explained what happened.

Many readers see this as a story about *trust*. The people had to choose whom to believe. Heiser read it as the first *rebellion*. Humans went against God's word, and so did the serpent. Readers across traditions agree the story is about a choice.

words.d: believing that someone is telling the truth and will do what is right
refusing to follow the one in charge

look.title: Whose Words to Believe
look.text: God said not to eat from one tree. The serpent said eating would make the people wise like God. The woman looked at the fruit and saw it was good to eat and nice to see. She had to choose between two voices.
look.prompt: What did the woman have to decide? Why do many readers call this a story about trust?

check.q: What did the serpent tell the woman would happen if she ate?
choices: She would be like God, knowing good and evil
check.why: In Genesis 3, the serpent said she would be like God, knowing good and evil.

check.q: What did the man and woman do when they heard God in the garden?
check.why: Genesis 3 says they hid when they heard God in the garden.

check.q: What did Heiser call this story?
check.why: Heiser read Eden as the first of three rebellions in Genesis.

lessons.title: Leaving the Garden
lessons.mainIdea: After the choice, the people had to leave Eden, and cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life.
reading: The choice changed things. Genesis 3 says work would now be hard and life would have pain. God made clothes of skins for the man and the woman. Many readers notice that God still cared for them, even after they chose wrongly.

Then the man and the woman had to leave the garden. Genesis 3:24 says God placed *cherubim* at the east of Eden. Cherubim are heavenly beings who guard holy places. A flaming sword turned every way to guard the path to the tree of life.

Heiser saw this as a great *loss*. People no longer lived in God's home. He thought much of the Bible after this tells how God works to bring people back. Many Christian and Jewish readers also see Eden as a home that people long for.

words.d: heavenly beings in the Bible who guard holy places
no longer having something you once had

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Picture the east side of the garden. Two people walk away wearing clothes God made for them. Behind them, heavenly guards stand at the gate. A bright, flaming sword turns this way and that. The tree of life is far inside.
look.prompt: Find one sign of loss and one sign of care in this picture.

check.q: Who did God place at the east of Eden, in Genesis 3:24?
check.why: Genesis 3:24 says God placed cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life.

check.q: What did God make for the man and woman before they left?
check.why: Genesis 3 says God made clothes of skins for them, which many readers see as a sign of care.

check.q: What did the flaming sword guard?
choices: The path to the tree of life
check.why: Genesis 3:24 says the flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life.

lessons.title: A Promise in Genesis 3:15
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 3:15 says a child of the woman will crush the serpent's head, and many readers see a promise in it.
reading: Before the people leave, God speaks to the serpent. Genesis 3:15 says there will be a struggle between the serpent and the woman. It also says there will be a struggle between their *offspring*. Offspring means children and the families that come after them.

The verse says the woman's offspring will bruise the serpent's head. The serpent will bruise his heel. A hurt heel heals. A crushed head does not. So many readers hear good news in this verse. They see a *promise* that evil will be beaten.

Many Christians read Genesis 3:15 as the first hint of Jesus. Heiser saw it as the start of a long story in the Bible. Many Jewish readers see a picture of the long struggle between people and snakes, or between people and wrongdoing. Each reading finds hope in the verse.

words.d: children and the families that come after them
words that say something good will surely happen

look.title: Head and Heel
look.text: God said to the serpent: I will make you and the woman enemies, and your children and her children enemies too. Her child will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.
look.cite: Genesis 3:15, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Which is hurt worse, the head or the heel? Why do many readers call this verse good news?

check.q: In Genesis 3:15, what will the woman's offspring do to the serpent?
check.why: Genesis 3:15 says the woman's offspring will bruise the serpent's head.

check.q: What does offspring mean?
choices: Children and the families that come after them
check.why: Offspring means children and the families that come after them.

check.q: How do many Christians read Genesis 3:15?
choices: As the first hint of Jesus
check.why: Many Christians read Genesis 3:15 as the first hint of Jesus.

review.q: Which three stories did Heiser call the three rebellions?
choices: Eden, the sons of God and Babel
Eden, the Flood and the Exodus
review.why: Heiser pointed to Eden (Genesis 3), the sons of God (Genesis 6) and Babel (Genesis 11).

review.q: Which book calls Eden the garden of God and the holy mountain of God?
review.why: Ezekiel 28:13–14 uses both phrases in a poem to the king of Tyre.

review.q: Which word is the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3?
review.why: Nachash is the Hebrew word for serpent; Heiser studied its related meanings.

review.q: Why did Heiser think the serpent was a shining one?
choices: Because it lived in the river
Because of word clues like bronze and omens, and Ezekiel 28
review.why: Heiser used word clues linked to nachash and the shining being of Ezekiel 28.

review.q: Where does the Bible call the old serpent the Devil and Satan?
review.why: Revelation 12:9 makes that link; Genesis 3 does not name the serpent.

review.q: How does a teaching-story reading see the serpent?
choices: As a member of God's council
As a snake in a story that teaches about choices
review.why: Some scholars read Genesis 3 as a teaching story in which a talking snake teaches a lesson.

review.q: What guarded the way to the tree of life after the people left Eden?
review.why: Genesis 3:24 says cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way.

review.q: Why do many readers hear good news in Genesis 3:15?
choices: Because a crushed head is worse than a bruised heel
Because the people stay in Eden
review.why: The woman's offspring bruises the serpent's head, which many readers see as a promise that evil will be beaten.

chapters.title: The Sons of God and the Flood
chapters.bigQuestion: Who were the sons of God in Genesis 6, and why do careful readers give different answers?

story.title: Four Verses, Three Ideas
story.kicker: A student reads four short verses aloud, and three classmates each hear something different.
paragraphs: Ms. Rivera's class was reading old stories from Genesis. Jamal raised his hand to read aloud. He found Genesis 6 and began. "The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair." He kept going to the end of verse 4. Then he looked up. "Who are the sons of God?"

Sofia answered first. "I think they are angels. In the book of Job, the sons of God are in heaven." Ben shook his head. "My uncle says they are people. They are the good family of Seth, Adam's son." Ana had a third idea. "Maybe they are kings. Kings in old times called themselves sons of gods."

The class got quiet. Everyone looked at Ms. Rivera. She did not tell them who was right. She wrote three headings on the board: Heavenly Beings, Family of Seth, Powerful Kings. "Each of you just named a reading that real scholars hold," she said. "People have discussed this for more than two thousand years."

"So how do we decide?" Jamal asked. Ms. Rivera smiled. "We look at the clues. What do these words mean in other places? Who read it this way first? What comes right after it?" She handed out a sheet. "A scholar named Michael Heiser studied these clues. Let's see what he found, and what others found too."
story.think: Sofia, Ben and Ana each gave a reason for their idea. Which kind of clue would help you most: other verses, old books or what happens next in the story?

lessons.title: What Genesis 6 Says
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 6:1–4 tells, in four short verses, of the sons of God, the daughters of men and the Nephilim.
reading: Genesis 6:1–4 is one of the shortest stories in the Bible. It has only four *verses*. A verse is one small numbered part of a chapter. Yet these four verses have caused more discussion than many long chapters.

The story says people were spreading over the earth. The *sons of God* saw that the daughters of men were beautiful. They took wives from among them. God then said people's days would be 120 years. This is in Genesis 6:3.

Verse 4 adds that the Nephilim were on the earth in those days. It says the children born then became mighty men of old, famous men. The verses do not explain much more. Readers have to put the clues together.

words.d: small numbered parts of a Bible chapter
the beings in Genesis 6:2 who took wives; readers disagree about who they were

look.title: Genesis 6:2
look.text: That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.
look.prompt: Who saw whom in this verse? What did they do next?

check.q: How many verses long is the story in Genesis 6:1–4?
check.why: Genesis 6:1–4 is four verses long.

check.q: In Genesis 6:2, who saw that the daughters of men were beautiful?
check.why: Genesis 6:2 says the sons of God saw the daughters of men.

check.q: What does Genesis 6:4 call the children born in those days?
choices: Mighty men of old, famous men
check.why: Genesis 6:4 calls them mighty men of old, men of renown, or famous men.

lessons.title: Who Are the Sons of God?
lessons.mainIdea: Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, the phrase sons of God is used for heavenly beings around God.
reading: One good way to understand a phrase is to find it in other places. The phrase sons of God appears in the book of *Job*. Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD. They gather in God's heavenly court.

Job 38:7 speaks of the time God made the earth. It says the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy. No people were there yet. So in Job, the sons of God are heavenly beings.

Heiser used these verses as his first clue. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he argued that sons of God means the same thing in Genesis 6. Other readers say a phrase can mean different things in different books. They look at the story around Genesis 6 instead.

words.d: a book of the Hebrew Bible about a man named Job and his troubles
a picture of God as a king with heavenly beings gathered around

look.title: Stars and Sons of God
look.text: When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
look.prompt: When were the sons of God shouting for joy? Why does that suggest they were not humans?

check.q: Which book uses sons of God for beings who gather before the LORD?
check.why: Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD.

check.q: In Job 38:7, when did the sons of God shout for joy?
check.why: Job 38:7 places their shout at the time God laid the earth's foundations, before people lived.

check.q: How do some other readers answer Heiser's clue from Job?
choices: They say a phrase can mean different things in different books
They say Job calls them giants
They say Job is not in the Bible
They say Job was written after Revelation
check.why: Other readers say one phrase can mean different things in different books.

lessons.title: The Nephilim
lessons.mainIdea: The Nephilim are named in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33; many translations call them giants.
reading: Genesis 6:4 names a group called the *Nephilim*. The King James Version translates the word as giants. Many newer Bibles keep the Hebrew name, Nephilim. The Bible does not describe what they looked like in Genesis.

The name appears again in Numbers 13:33. Spies sent into Canaan came back with a report. They said they saw the Nephilim there. They said they felt as small as grasshoppers next to them. So the Bible links the name with very tall people.

Readers disagree about what the name means. Many connect it to a Hebrew word meaning to fall. Heiser thought it more likely came from an *Aramaic* word meaning giant. Aramaic is a language close to Hebrew. Either way, the story stays short and calm.

words.d: a group named in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33; many translations call them giants
an old language close to Hebrew, used in parts of the Bible

look.title: Two Ideas About a Name
look.text: Idea 1: Nephilim comes from the Hebrew word naphal, to fall, so it means fallen ones. Idea 2: Nephilim comes from an Aramaic word for giant, so it means giants. Heiser preferred Idea 2. Many readers prefer Idea 1.
look.prompt: Which verse in Numbers could someone use to support Idea 2? Explain.

check.q: How does the King James Version translate Nephilim in Genesis 6:4?
check.why: The King James Version translates Nephilim as giants.

check.q: In Numbers 13:33, how did the spies say they felt next to the Nephilim?
check.why: Numbers 13:33 says the spies felt like grasshoppers beside them.

check.q: Where did Heiser think the name Nephilim came from?
check.why: Heiser thought Nephilim more likely came from an Aramaic word meaning giant.

lessons.title: Reading One: Heavenly Beings
lessons.mainIdea: The oldest Jewish readings, in 1 Enoch and Jubilees, say the sons of God were heavenly beings, and Heiser agreed.
reading: The oldest known writings that explain Genesis 6 are Jewish books from before the time of Jesus. One is *1 Enoch*. Its first part, the Book of the Watchers, was likely written about 300 to 200 BCE. It calls the sons of God *Watchers*, heavenly beings who came down to earth.

1 Enoch 6 says two hundred Watchers came down on Mount Hermon. Another old book, Jubilees, also says the angels of the Lord took wives. Today 1 Enoch is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches. But many ancient Jews read it.

Heiser took this reading. In Reversing Hermon (2017), he argued that the first readers of Genesis would have heard sons of God as heavenly beings. He saw their choice as the second rebellion, after Eden.

words.d: an old Jewish book, in the Bible of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches, that retells Genesis 6
1 Enoch's name for the heavenly beings who came down to earth

look.title: When Readers Explained Genesis 6
look.cite: Common scholarly dates: 1 Enoch 1–36 c. 300–200 BCE; Jubilees c. 160 BCE; Julius Africanus c. 220 CE; Augustine, City of God c. 420 CE
look.prompt: Which reading is written down first? About how many years passed before the line of Seth reading appears?

check.q: What does 1 Enoch call the sons of God?
check.why: 1 Enoch calls them Watchers, heavenly beings who came down to earth.

check.q: Which churches include 1 Enoch in their Bible today?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

check.q: In which book did Heiser argue this reading, as named in the lesson?
check.why: The lesson names Heiser's Reversing Hermon (2017).

lessons.title: Reading Two: The Line of Seth
lessons.mainIdea: Another reading says the sons of God were Seth's faithful family marrying into Cain's family.
reading: Genesis 4 and 5 tell of two families. One comes from *Cain*, the son of Adam who killed his brother Abel. The other comes from *Seth*, a son born to Adam and Eve later. Genesis 4:26 says people began to call on the name of the LORD in Seth's time.

In the early 200s CE, a Christian writer named Julius Africanus read Genesis 6 this way. The sons of God were Seth's faithful family. The daughters of men came from Cain's family. Around 420 CE, Augustine, a famous church leader, taught this reading in his book City of God.

This became the most common Christian reading for centuries. Many still hold it. They point out that angels are not said to marry in Matthew 22:30. Heiser disagreed. He noted Genesis never calls Seth's family sons of God.

words.d: a son of Adam and Eve; one reading says his family were the sons of God
a son of Adam and Eve; one reading says the daughters of men came from his family

look.title: Two Families
look.text: Family 1: Seth's line, where Genesis 4:26 says people called on the LORD. Family 2: Cain's line, which Genesis 4 says built a city and made tools. The line of Seth reading says Family 1 married into Family 2.
look.prompt: What does the line of Seth reading think went wrong in Genesis 6?

check.q: Who taught the line of Seth reading in the book City of God?
check.why: Augustine taught this reading in City of God, around 420 CE.

check.q: In this reading, who were the daughters of men?
check.why: The line of Seth reading says the daughters of men came from Cain's family.

check.q: What did Heiser point out against this reading?
choices: Genesis never calls Seth's family sons of God
check.why: Heiser noted that Genesis never calls Seth's family sons of God.

lessons.title: Reading Three: Powerful Kings
lessons.mainIdea: A third reading says the sons of God were powerful human rulers who took whatever wives they wanted.
reading: In the ancient world, some *kings* said they were children of gods. In Egypt, the pharaoh was called a son of the sun god Ra. So some readers think the sons of God in Genesis 6 were proud rulers.

Some Jewish teachers of the early centuries CE read it this way. An old Aramaic translation of Genesis, the Targum Onqelos, calls them the sons of great men. In this reading, the sin was *pride*. Rulers took any women they chose.

Some modern scholars also hold this view. They note that verse 4 calls the children mighty men and famous men, words often used for warriors. Heiser disagreed. He thought the pull of Job and 1 Enoch was too strong.

words.d: rulers of a land; one reading says the sons of God were kings
thinking you are better or more important than others

look.title: A Ruler's Title
look.text: Imagine an ancient ruler carving his name in stone: Son of the Sun God, Mighty King. Now read Genesis 6:2 again: the sons of God took wives of all which they chose. The kings reading asks whether these could be the same kind of people.
look.prompt: What does the kings reading say was wrong with what the sons of God did?

check.q: Which ruler was called a son of the sun god Ra?
check.why: In Egypt, the pharaoh was called a son of the sun god Ra.

check.q: What does the Targum Onqelos call the sons of God?
check.why: The Targum Onqelos, an old Aramaic translation, calls them the sons of great men.

check.q: In the kings reading, what was the wrong they did?
choices: Pride, taking any women they chose
check.why: The kings reading says proud rulers took any women they chose.

lessons.title: Clues From the New Testament
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser pointed to 2 Peter 2 and Jude 6, which speak of angels who sinned, near the story of Noah.
reading: Heiser also looked at the New Testament. 2 Peter 2:4 speaks of angels who sinned. It says God put them in a dark place to wait for judgment. The Greek word used there for that place is *Tartarus*.
The next verse, 2 Peter 2:5, talks about Noah and the Flood. Jude 6 tells of angels who left their proper home. Heiser argued that both letters follow the heavenly beings reading, like 1 Enoch.

Readers who hold the line of Seth reading answer differently. They say these verses could be about a different fall of angels. They say they do not have to point to Genesis 6. Heiser thought the link to Noah made Genesis 6 the best fit.

words.d: the Greek word in 2 Peter 2:4 for the dark place where angels who sinned are kept
a time when someone decides what is right and what should happen

look.title: Angels in Jude
look.text: The angels who did not keep their first place, but left their own home, God is keeping in chains in darkness until the great day of judgment.
look.cite: Jude 6, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What did these angels leave? Why might Heiser connect this to Genesis 6?

check.q: Which verse comes right after 2 Peter 2:4 and mentions Noah?
check.why: 2 Peter 2:5 speaks of Noah and the Flood, right after the angels who sinned in 2:4.

check.q: What is Tartarus?
choices: The Greek word in 2 Peter 2:4 for the dark place where angels who sinned are kept
check.why: 2 Peter 2:4 uses the Greek word Tartarus for that dark place.

check.q: How do line of Seth readers answer Heiser's New Testament clue?
choices: They say the verses are about kings
They say Noah was an angel
They say the verses could be about a different fall of angels
They say 2 Peter is not in the Bible
check.why: Line of Seth readers say these verses may describe a different fall of angels.

lessons.title: Putting Heiser's Clues Together
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser built his view from several clues together: Job, 1 Enoch, the New Testament and the mighty children.
reading: Heiser did not rest his view on one verse. He put several *clues* together. First, sons of God means heavenly beings in Job. Second, the oldest Jewish readers said so. Third, 2 Peter and Jude seem to agree.

Fourth, he pointed to the children. Genesis 6:4 calls them mighty men of old. Numbers 13:33 links the Nephilim with very tall people. Heiser thought ordinary human marriages would not explain this. He saw a heavenly *boundary* being crossed.

Readers who disagree weigh the clues differently. Some give most weight to Matthew 22:30, about angels not marrying. Some trust later church teaching. Studying this debate shows how scholars build a case from many clues.

words.d: pieces of information that help answer a question
a line that marks where one thing ends and another begins

look.title: Heiser's Four Clues
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (2015) and Reversing Hermon (2017), summarized
look.prompt: Which clue comes from outside the Bible used by most churches? Which clue is about the children?

check.q: Which clue is about what the oldest Jewish readers said?
check.why: 1 Enoch and Jubilees are the oldest Jewish readings Heiser pointed to.

check.q: What did Heiser think was crossed in Genesis 6?
check.why: Heiser saw a boundary between heaven and earth being crossed.

check.q: Which verse do many who disagree give the most weight?
check.why: Many who disagree point to Matthew 22:30, about angels not marrying.

lessons.title: Why the Flood Came
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 6:5–7 says people's hearts had turned to wrong, and God decided to send a flood.
reading: Next comes Genesis 6:5. It says the LORD saw that people's *wickedness* was great. Every thought of their hearts was only evil all the time. Genesis 6:6 says this grieved God in his heart.

So God decided to send a flood. Many readers see the reason in verse 5, the wrong that people did. Heiser agreed that human wrong was part of it. He also thought Genesis 6:1–4 was placed there on purpose, as part of the reason.

Genesis 6:8 then says something hopeful. "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." *Grace* means kindness that someone did not earn. In the middle of a sad chapter, the story turns to one family.

words.d: doing what is wrong and harmful
kindness and favor that someone did not earn

look.title: Noah Found Grace
look.text: But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.
look.prompt: The word But turns the story. What changes after this verse?

check.q: What does Genesis 6:5 say the LORD saw?
check.why: Genesis 6:5 says the LORD saw that people's wickedness was great.

check.q: Who found grace in the eyes of the LORD?
check.why: Genesis 6:8 says Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.

check.q: What did Heiser think about Genesis 6:1–4 and the Flood?
choices: That the Flood was about Babel
That the four verses were placed there on purpose, as part of the reason
check.why: Heiser thought Genesis 6:1–4 was placed before the Flood on purpose, as part of the reason.

lessons.title: Noah and the Ark
lessons.mainIdea: God told Noah to build a huge ark, and Noah's family and the animals were kept safe inside.
reading: Genesis 6:9 calls Noah a just man who walked with God. God told Noah to build an *ark*. An ark is a large boat shaped like a box. Genesis 6:15 gives its size: 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide and 30 cubits high.
A *cubit* was the length from an elbow to the tip of the middle finger. That is about 18 inches. So the ark was about 450 feet long. That is longer than a football field.

Noah, his wife, his three sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives went inside. Animals went in too, by pairs. Genesis 7:12 says rain fell for forty days and forty nights. The story says everyone inside the ark was kept safe.

words.d: a large box-shaped boat; in Genesis, the boat Noah built
an old measure, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 18 inches

look.title: Numbers in the Flood Story
rows: Days the waters rose over the earth
Noah's age when the Flood began
look.prompt: How many times longer was the ark than it was wide?

check.q: How long was the ark, according to Genesis 6:15?
check.why: Genesis 6:15 says the ark was 300 cubits long.

check.q: What is a cubit?
choices: The length from elbow to middle fingertip
check.why: A cubit is the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 18 inches.

check.q: Who were Noah's three sons?
check.why: Genesis names Noah's sons as Shem, Ham and Japheth.

lessons.title: The Rainbow Promise
lessons.mainIdea: After the Flood, God made a covenant with Noah and set the rainbow as its sign.
reading: After the waters went down, Noah and his family came out of the ark. Genesis 9 says God made a *covenant* with Noah. A covenant is a serious promise that binds two sides together. God promised never again to send a flood to destroy the earth.
God gave a sign of this promise. Genesis 9:13 says, "I do set my bow in the cloud." The bow is a *rainbow*. The story says God will see the rainbow and remember the promise to every living thing.

Heiser saw the Flood as a fresh start after the second rebellion. Many Jewish and Christian readers see the rainbow as a sign of God's patience with the world. The story of rebellion does not end here. Genesis 11 tells of Babel next.

words.d: a serious promise that binds two sides together
the colored bow in the sky; in Genesis 9, the sign of God's promise

look.title: The Bow in the Cloud
look.text: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
look.prompt: The word token means sign. What is the bow a sign of?

check.q: What is a covenant?
choices: A serious promise that binds two sides together
check.why: A covenant is a serious promise that binds two sides; God made one with Noah in Genesis 9.

check.q: What did God promise in the covenant with Noah?
choices: Never again to send a flood to destroy the earth
check.why: Genesis 9 says God promised never again to destroy the earth with a flood.

check.q: Which story in Genesis comes next, after the Flood, in Heiser's three rebellions?
check.why: Babel in Genesis 11 is the third rebellion, after the Flood.

review.q: Where is the story of the sons of God and the daughters of men?
Which reading did Heiser hold about the sons of God?
review.why: Heiser read them as heavenly beings, like 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

review.q: Which reading was taught by Julius Africanus and Augustine?
review.why: Julius Africanus and Augustine taught that the sons of God were Seth's family.

review.q: Which book of the Bible uses sons of God for beings who shouted for joy when the earth was made?
review.why: Job 38:7 says all the sons of God shouted for joy.

review.q: In which book do the spies say they felt like grasshoppers next to the Nephilim?
review.why: Numbers 13:33 tells the spies' report about the Nephilim.

review.q: What is the difference between the heavenly beings reading and the kings reading?
choices: One says heavenly beings, the other says proud human rulers
One is about Noah, the other about Eden
One says angels, the other says Seth's family
review.why: The heavenly beings reading sees spirit beings; the kings reading sees proud human rulers.

review.q: What does Genesis 6:8 say about Noah?
choices: He was one of the Nephilim
He found grace in the eyes of the LORD
review.why: Genesis 6:8 says Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.

review.q: What was the sign of God's covenant with Noah?
review.why: Genesis 9:13 says God set his bow in the cloud as a sign of the covenant.
